title: The French Defense
summary: Two chains, and both bases under fire

steps.title: A Center Pawn, One Move Late
steps.text:
{{e4}} {{e6}}. Black answers a center pawn with a quiet one, because the next move is the point: {{d4}} {{d5}}, and now Black has a pawn abreast of White's with another behind it holding it up.

The cost sits on c8. That bishop's diagonal runs straight into Black's own pawn on e6, and freeing it can take twenty moves. Paris beat London by post with this in 1834, and the opening has carried the French name ever since.

steps.title: Aim at the Bottom
steps.text:
White pushed past, and the pawns are locked. White's chain runs d4 to e5 and points at Black's kingside; Black's runs e6 to d5 and points at White's queenside. Each army attacks where its own pawns are aimed.

Black's bottom pawn is e6, behind everything. White's is d4, out in the open. The pawn on c5 and the knight on c6 already hit it, while the pawn on c3, the knight on f3 and the queen on d1 hold it up. Two against three, and it is Black's move.

> A pawn chain is only as strong as the pawn at the bottom.

steps.prompt: Aim a third piece at d4 from behind your own c-pawn — pick the square that also stares at b2.
steps.hint: Find the piece that hits b2 now and hits d4 the moment your c-pawn trades itself off.

steps.title: The Other French
steps.text:
Same two opening moves, a different quarrel. White defended the e-pawn with a knight on c3 rather than pushing it, Black's dark bishop came to b4 and pinned that knight against the king, and White pushed past anyway. Now {{a3}} asks the bishop what it intends.

It does not retreat. {{Bxc3+}} {{bxc3}}: Black hands over a bishop, and White's b-pawn is dragged onto the c-file, where two white pawns now stand and can never be untangled.

steps.title: Reading the Receipt
steps.text:
Both sides know what they bought. White owns two bishops against one, room on the kingside, and a half-open b-file for the rook in the corner; Black's dark squares now have no bishop to look after them.

Black owns the healthier pawns and a standing target: the pawn on c3 is defended by nothing at all. {{Qa5}} arrives on the diagonal that ends at the white king, and White must spend a move on {{Bd2}} to prop the pawn up.

steps.title: Three Squares, Two Answers
steps.text:
The knight on g8 has three squares, and two of them are answered before it lands.

f6 is covered by the pawn on e5, so a knight there loses a piece for a pawn. h6 is legal, but the bishop on c1 stares straight down at it, and the trade there leaves Black's king shelter in ruins.

That leaves one square. From there the knight is a single hop from f5, where it attacks d4 all over again and where no white pawn covers it yet.

steps.prompt: Bring out the knight beside your king on the one square that leaves it a single hop from f5.
steps.hint: One of its squares is covered by a pawn, and one invites a trade that wrecks the cover in front of your king; the third is the move.
